subject: Social Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Ancient Land, Many Names: Launching the Inquiry
periods.section_anchor: Introduction — India as an ancient land with changing names
periods.visual_aids: Political outline map of the Indian Subcontinent displayed on the board

time_bands.activity: Students write on a slip of paper every name they know for India — in any language, from any source. After two minutes of silent individual listing, pairs share their lists. The teacher collects responses and writes a composite class inventory on the board, grouping names visually: Indian-origin names on the left, foreign-origin names on the right.

The teacher poses two anchoring questions: 'Why would the same land carry so many different names?' and 'Who was doing the naming — the people living here, or those arriving from outside?' Students examine the outline map and note that the Subcontinent is bordered by sea on three sides and mountains to the north. They discuss in pairs how this geography might have shaped how the land was perceived and named by both insiders and outsiders.

Students return to their slip and mark each name with 'I' (Indian origin) or 'F' (foreign origin), then write one sentence explaining how they decided. The teacher invites three to four students to share their reasoning, drawing out the idea that names are evidence of a historical relationship — and that the chapter will trace how these names changed across thousands of years through texts, inscriptions, and travellers' accounts.

The teacher introduces the chapter's organising structure — two inquiry threads: names Indians gave their land, and names foreigners gave it — and writes both headings on the board. Students copy the two questions into their notebooks as the chapter's guiding framework, leaving space beneath each to add evidence as the chapter progresses.

periods.section_context: Indian Subcontinent, changing names, texts, inscriptions, travellers' accounts
periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit invites students to treat naming as a historical act rather than a fixed label, setting up the chapter's central inquiry without requiring any prior content. A common confusion to pre-empt: students often assume 'India' has always been the land's name — make explicit that the name 'India' is itself a foreign coinage whose origin the chapter will trace. The pair-share on geography and naming keeps the discussion grounded in evidence rather than free association.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can frame historical questions about why place-names change across time and who does the naming.

periods.activity_title: Sapta Sindhava: Reading the Rig Veda's Regional Name
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Rig Veda and 'Sapta Sindhava'
materials: Printed or projected excerpt of the Rig Veda reference to 'Sapta Sindhava'
periods.visual_aids: Simple sketch-map on the board showing the northwest region of the Subcontinent and the Indus / Sindhu river

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'Sapta Sindhava' on the board and asks students to break the compound: 'Sapta' means seven, 'Sindhava' relates to 'Sindhu'. Students brainstorm what 'land of the seven rivers' might look like on a map. The teacher then draws a quick sketch showing the northwest of the Subcontinent and marks the Sindhu/Indus, explaining that 'Sindhu' named both the river and rivers in general in this ancient text.

Students read the short passage about the Rig Veda's age and the term 'Sapta Sindhava'. The teacher poses: 'This is described as a regional name, not a name for the whole Subcontinent — what does that tell us about how people understood their land several thousand years ago?' Students write a two-sentence response and share with a partner. The teacher draws out the point that naming was partial and local before it became pan-subcontinental.

Students work individually on a source-analysis task: given that the Rig Veda is 'India's oldest text', they answer — (a) What kind of source is the Rig Veda? (b) What does the name 'Sapta Sindhava' tell us about which part of the Subcontinent was being described? (c) What does 'Sindhu' as a root word suggest might happen to this name when it reaches other languages? Students write responses in full sentences.

The teacher takes responses to question (c) from two or three students, noting predictions on the board without confirming or denying them — this plants a question the chapter's foreign-names section will later answer. Students add 'Sapta Sindhava — Rig Veda — northwest/seven rivers' to their chapter framework notes.

periods.section_context: Rig Veda, Sapta Sindhava, Sindhu, seven rivers, northwest region
periods.teacher_notes: The Rig Veda passage introduces the principle that ancient names were regional and source-specific — a conceptual anchor for everything the chapter traces afterward. A likely confusion: students may conflate 'Sindhu' (the river / rivers in general) with 'Sindhava' (the people or land of the Sindhu) — clarify this explicitly when breaking down the compound. The deliberate cliff-hanger on the word's travel to other languages builds motivated curiosity for the foreign-names thread.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify a named ancient text as a historical source and explain what kind of evidence it provides about a region.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain why the earliest recorded name for the Subcontinent was regional rather than pan-subcontinental.

periods.activity_title: Mapping the Mahabharata's India: Regional Names Across the Subcontinent
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Mahabharata regional names and Fig. 5.4
materials: Printed or projected reproduction of Fig. 5.4 (Mahabharata-era regional map)
Blank outline maps of the Subcontinent (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Fig. 5.4 from the chapter projected or drawn large on the board showing Mahabharata-era regions

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays Fig. 5.4 and reads aloud the list of regions from the Mahabharata: Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha, Kerala, and others. Students are asked to listen and mentally match each to a modern state or region they know. After the reading, students call out their matches while the teacher annotates the map on the board.

Students receive blank outline maps and, using Fig. 5.4 as reference, mark and label at least six Mahabharata-era regions with their approximate modern equivalents in brackets — for example, 'Kashmira (Kashmir)', 'Vanga (Bengal)', 'Pragjyotisha (Assam)'. They then answer in writing: 'What does the spread of these regions across the entire Subcontinent tell us about how people who composed the Mahabharata understood the land they were describing?'

The teacher leads a brief discussion using two probing questions: 'Do these regional names cover the whole Subcontinent, or only parts of it?' and 'Why might a single text contain names for so many different regions?' Students are guided to see that the Mahabharata's authors had a pan-subcontinental awareness, even while naming individual regions.

Students add a one-line entry to their framework notes: 'Mahabharata — lists regional names from Kashmir to Kerala to Assam to Kutch — shows pan-subcontinental geographic awareness.' Their annotated maps are kept in their notebooks for reference.

periods.section_context: Mahabharata, Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha, Kerala, Fig. 5.4
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the Rig Veda's single northwest designation, this unit shifts to the Mahabharata's pan-subcontinental regional vocabulary — a qualitative leap in the scope of naming. A common confusion: students may assume the Mahabharata is primarily a geographical text; clarify that its listing of regions appears within a literary-epic context, making it an indirect but rich historical source. The map-annotation task requires students to translate textual names into spatial reasoning, which is the unit's core cognitive move.

competency_edges.competency_text: Mapping textual geographical descriptions onto physical geography
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can locate ancient regional names from a historical text onto an outline map and match them to contemporary geographical areas.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how the range of regional names in the Mahabharata reflects an expanding geographic awareness of the Subcontinent over time.

periods.activity_title: Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa: Whole-Subcontinent Names Emerge
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, and Ashoka's inscription
materials: Brief printed or projected passage on Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, and Ashoka's inscription
periods.visual_aids: Timeline on the board: Rig Veda → Mahabharata (few centuries BCE onward) → Ashoka c. 250 BCE

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa' on the board and unpacks both: 'Bharatavarsha' = country of the Bharatas (Bharata first appears in the Rig Veda as a Vedic group; several kings named Bharata appear later); 'Jambudvipa' = island of the fruit of the jamun tree, a tree native to India. Students note both meanings and discuss: 'What does each name emphasise — people, place, or nature?'

The teacher introduces Ashoka's inscription (c. 250 BCE): Ashoka used 'Jambudvipa' to describe the whole of India — which at that time included present-day Bangladesh, Pakistan, and parts of Afghanistan. Students analyse: 'What does it mean that a political ruler chose a nature-based name like Jambudvipa for his empire?' and 'How does Ashoka's use of this name constitute a type of historical evidence different from a literary text?' Students write responses.

Students construct a short comparison: in a two-column table (columns: Bharatavarsha / Jambudvipa), they write the meaning, the source it appears in, what it refers to, and what type of source that is. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'Which name ties India to its people? Which ties it to its natural environment?'

The teacher closes by updating the class timeline on the board, adding Ashoka's inscription at c. 250 BCE and noting that the Subcontinent now has at least two whole-land names alongside its regional ones. Students update their framework notes: 'Bharatavarsha — country of the Bharatas (Mahabharata); Jambudvipa — land of the jamun tree (Mahabharata + Ashoka inscription c. 250 BCE).'

periods.section_context: Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, Mahabharata, Ashoka inscription, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Afghanistan
periods.teacher_notes: Having mapped the Mahabharata's regional vocabulary, this unit shows the same text coining whole-Subcontinent names — a key step in the chapter's change-tracing arc. A frequent confusion: students conflate 'Jambudvipa' with a mythological concept; ground it firmly in Ashoka's epigraphic use to show it was a real administrative and political designation. The two-column comparison sharpens the distinction between people-centred and nature-centred naming conventions.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare what a literary source and an epigraphic inscription each reveal about the geographical conception of the Subcontinent.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how the emergence of whole-Subcontinent names like Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa marks a change from regional to pan-subcontinental naming.

periods.activity_title: The Vishnu Purana's Boundaries: Reading a Geographic Definition
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — Vishnu Purana verse and geographical boundaries
materials: Printed or projected Sanskrit verse in translation from the Vishnu Purana
Printed or projected outline map of the Subcontinent showing the Himalayas and surrounding oceans
periods.visual_aids: Outline map of the Subcontinent with the Himalayas labelled to the north and the Indian Ocean to the south

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the Vishnu Purana verse: 'The country that lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is called Bharata.' Students listen with eyes closed and then sketch from memory the geographical shape this description produces — a landmass bounded by water in the south and mountains in the north. They compare their sketch to the outline map displayed.

The teacher poses the 'Think About It' questions: 'Which mountains are called the snowy mountains?' and 'Is this geographical description accurate for the Indian Subcontinent as we know it today?' Students examine the outline map, identify the Himalayas, and then evaluate the verse — writing two sentences on what the description captures correctly and what it leaves out or simplifies.

The teacher introduces the ancient Tamil poem's parallel description: a king's fame extending from Cape Kumari in the south to the great mountain in the north, from the eastern ocean to the western ocean. Students answer: 'Does this Tamil poem describe the same geography as the Vishnu Purana verse? What does it add?' They mark Cape Kumari (southernmost tip) on their maps.

The teacher draws out the comparative insight: two sources from different languages and regions — Sanskrit and Tamil — converge on the same geographical definition of Bharata. Students record in their notebooks: 'Vishnu Purana verse + ancient Tamil poem — both define Bharata by ocean (south), mountains (north), and two oceans (east/west) — showing a shared geographic conception across regions.'

periods.section_context: Vishnu Purana verse, snowy mountains, Himalayas, Cape Kumari, Tamil poem, Bharata boundaries
periods.teacher_notes: Having established the names Bharatavarsha and Jambudvipa, this unit examines how ancient Indians defined the Subcontinent's physical extent through two different literary traditions. A common confusion: students may not immediately place 'snowy mountains' as the Himalayas — give them a moment with the map before confirming. The convergence between the Sanskrit verse and the Tamil poem is a conceptually rich moment: it demonstrates that a shared geographical imagination of Bharata transcended regional and linguistic boundaries.

competency_edges.competency_text: Mapping textual geographical descriptions onto physical geography
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate whether a textual geographical boundary description matches the physical features of the Indian Subcontinent.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare two sources from different literary traditions to show they encode a shared geographical conception of the Subcontinent.

periods.activity_title: 'Bharat' in the Constitution: A Living Name from Ancient Roots
periods.section_anchor: How Indians Named India — 'Bharat' in the Indian Constitution
materials: Printed or projected reproduction of the Indian Constitution's opening page (Article 1)
periods.visual_aids: Projected image of the Indian Constitution's first page with Article 1 highlighted

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays the Constitution's opening page and asks students to locate and read aloud Article 1: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.' Students are asked: 'Why do you think the Constitution uses two names in the same sentence?' They write a one-sentence hypothesis before any discussion begins.

The teacher draws a quick tracing on the board: 'Bharata' first appears in the Rig Veda as a Vedic group → kings named Bharata in later literature → 'Bharatavarsha' in the Mahabharata → 'Bharata' in the Vishnu Purana verse → 'Bharat' in the Constitution. Students copy this chain and annotate each step with the source type (oral hymn, epic, Purana, legal document). They then answer: 'What does placing this ancient name in the Constitution's first line communicate about how India's founders understood the country's identity?'

Students write a short reflective response (four to five sentences) to the prompt: 'The Constitution was written in 1949–50. The name Bharat is several thousand years old. What does their coexistence in a single sentence tell us about continuity and change in how India defines itself?' Students share with a partner and refine before the class hears two or three responses.

The teacher closes the 'How Indians Named India' thread by pointing to the board inventory of names — Sapta Sindhava, Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, Bharata/Bharat — and asking students to arrange them in the order they were recorded, noting what type of source each comes from. This consolidation prepares the class to shift to the foreign-naming thread.

periods.section_context: Indian Constitution Article 1, Bharat, Bharata, Rig Veda, continuity of naming
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the Vishnu Purana's geographical definition of Bharata and its Tamil parallel, this unit closes the Indian-naming thread by showing the name's continuity into the present legal document. A common confusion: students may assume 'Bharat' and 'India' are simply synonyms — the constitutional pairing 'India, that is Bharat' is itself the evidence that they are historically distinct names that came to refer to the same nation. The reflective writing task asks students to hold continuity and change simultaneously, which is the chapter's core analytical demand.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a chronological chain showing how a name travelled from ancient texts to a modern constitutional document.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain what it means for an ancient name to appear in a modern legal source, using the Constitution as evidence of continuity.

periods.activity_title: Persian Names: Hind, Hidu, Hindu — Geography, Not Religion
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Persian names: Hind, Hidu, Hindu
materials: Etymology chain written on a strip of paper or projected: Sindhu → Hindhu → Hind/Hidu/Hindu
periods.visual_aids: Etymology chain displayed on the board: Sindhu → Hindhu → Hind / Hidu / Hindu

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by asking: 'If you were a Persian traveller arriving in the 6th century BCE and you crossed a great river the locals called 'Sindhu', what would you call the land on the other side?' Students guess. The teacher then explains: the Persians pronounced 'S' as 'H', so 'Sindhu' became 'Hindhu', and the land beyond became 'Hind', 'Hidu', or 'Hindu'. The teacher writes the full chain on the board.

Students read the passage explaining that in ancient Persian usage 'Hindu' is a purely geographical term — it designates the people and land of the Indus region, not a religious group. The teacher poses: 'What kind of evidence do we have for this claim — inscriptions, texts, or both?' and 'Why does this distinction between a geographical and a religious use of the word matter for understanding history?' Students write two-sentence answers.

Students practise the source-analysis skill: given the information that a Persian emperor campaigned into the Indus region in the 6th century BCE and that Persian records thereafter used 'Hind/Hindu', they answer — (a) What type of source is a Persian inscription? (b) What does it record about how Persians understood this land? (c) How is the Persian name derived from an Indian name? The teacher takes responses and records key answers on the board.

Students add to their framework notes: 'Persian names: Hind, Hidu, Hindu — derived from Sindhu (S→H sound shift) — 6th century BCE onwards — purely geographical in ancient usage.' They also note the source types used (Persian inscriptions, Persian records) and update their running etymology chain begun in an earlier unit.

periods.section_context: Persian names, Hind, Hidu, Hindu, Sindhu, 6th century BCE, geographical term
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced how Indians named their land up to the Constitution, this unit opens the foreign-naming thread with the Persians' derivation from 'Sindhu' — the same root word students predicted would travel when they studied the Rig Veda. A critical confusion to address directly: 'Hindu' in its ancient Persian context is a geographical designator, not a religious one; students with prior exposure to the word in its religious sense need explicit clarification that historical meaning and contemporary meaning are not the same. The source-analysis sub-task reinforces that Persian inscriptions are a specific and distinct evidence type.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between the geographical and religious uses of a historical term by examining the source in which it appears.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how a phonological shift transformed an Indian river name into a foreign name for the Subcontinent.

periods.activity_title: Greek Names: Indoi and Indike — How 'H' Became 'I'
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Greek names: Indoi, Indike
materials: Extended etymology chain: Sindhu → Hindhu → Indoi / Indike
periods.visual_aids: Extended etymology chain on the board: Sindhu → Hindhu → Indoi / Indike (with annotation: Greek has no 'H' sound)

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes on the board: 'Persian: Hindu → Greek: Indoi'. Students are asked: 'What changed between the Persian and Greek versions of this name?' Give students one minute to examine the chain, then take responses. The teacher confirms: Greek did not have the 'H' sound, so the Persians' 'Hindhu' became 'Indoi' or 'Indike' in Greek — a sound-system constraint, not a choice.

Students read the passage on the Greek names and then construct the full three-step etymology chain in their notebooks: Sindhu (Indian) → Hindhu (Persian) → Indoi / Indike (Greek). Below the chain, they write one sentence explaining why each step changed the word and what caused the change (meaning vs. sound system). The teacher circulates and checks that students are identifying linguistic cause, not arbitrary change.

The teacher poses a broader analytical question: 'What does the fact that both Persian and Greek names for India derive from a single Indian river name tell us about where early foreign knowledge of India began geographically?' Students discuss in pairs and then write a four-sentence response. The teacher guides them to see that early foreign contact with the Subcontinent began at its northwest — the Indus — and that the name spread from there.

Students update their framework notes with the Greek names and source types. The teacher previews the next step: 'The chain doesn't stop at Greek — we will trace it onward to China.' Students note the open question: 'What will Chinese do with Indoi/Indike or with Hindhu?'

periods.section_context: Greek names, Indoi, Indike, sound shift, Sindhu etymology chain, northwest entry point
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the Persian derivation from Sindhu, this unit follows the same root word one step further as Greek borrowed from Persian — demonstrating that names carry their history inside them. A common confusion: students sometimes think Greek speakers heard the Indian name directly; clarify that the Greek chain runs through Persian, not straight from Sanskrit. The analytical question about where early foreign knowledge of India began is the unit's highest-demand move, asking students to infer geographical history from etymological evidence.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a multi-step etymology chain and explain the linguistic and historical reason for each transformation.

periods.activity_title: Chinese Names: Yintu, Yindu, Tianzhu — Reverence and Etymology
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Chinese names: Yintu, Yindu, Tianzhu
materials: Chinese etymology chain: Sindhu → Hindhu → Indu → Yindu, and separate derivation for Tianzhu
periods.visual_aids: Two etymology chains on the board: (1) Sindhu → Hindhu → Indu → Yintu/Yindu; (2) Sindhu → ... → Tianzhu with the gloss 'heavenly master'

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the Chinese names 'Yintu', 'Yindu', and 'Tianzhu' on the board and asks students to identify which one looks most different from all the names seen so far. Students note 'Tianzhu'. The teacher explains the chain for Yintu/Yindu: Sindhu → Hindhu → Indu → Yintu/Yindu (another phonological adaptation). Students copy the chain.

The teacher introduces Tianzhu: it also derives from Sindhu, but in Chinese it could additionally be read as 'heavenly master', reflecting reverence for India as the birthplace of the Buddha. Students analyse: 'Why might the Chinese give India a name that means heavenly master? What does this tell us about the relationship between ancient China and India beyond just geography?' Students write three sentences connecting the name's meaning to the cultural relationship it encodes.

Students compare all foreign names studied so far — Persian (Hind/Hindu), Greek (Indoi/Indike), Chinese (Yintu/Yindu/Tianzhu) — in a three-row table they construct in their notebooks: columns are Language, Name(s), Root, and What the name reveals beyond the etymology. The teacher circulates, prompting: 'Does Tianzhu reveal something the other names do not? What?'

Students share their 'What the name reveals' column for Tianzhu. The teacher draws out the key insight: while most foreign names for India are purely geographical derivations, Tianzhu is also a cultural statement — it encodes India's status as a centre of Buddhist learning in the ancient Chinese imagination. Students add this insight to their framework notes.

periods.section_context: Chinese names, Yintu, Yindu, Tianzhu, heavenly master, Buddha, Sindhu etymology chain
periods.teacher_notes: Having followed the Sindhu chain through Persian and Greek, this unit extends it to Chinese — where a second name, Tianzhu, introduces a cultural dimension absent from purely geographical derivations. A common confusion: students may treat all three Chinese names as equivalent; distinguish Yintu/Yindu (phonological chain from Sindhu) from Tianzhu (same root but carrying an additional cultural reading). The comparative table is the unit's central analytical product and should capture the qualitative difference Tianzhu represents.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding India's cultural reach and influence on neighbouring civilisations
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how a foreign name for India encodes a cultural relationship, not only a geographical derivation.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can extend a multi-step etymology chain to a new language and explain how cultural context shaped one variant's meaning beyond phonological change.

periods.activity_title: Xuanzang's Journey: A Pilgrim as Historical Source
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — Xuanzang sidebar ('Don't Miss Out')
materials: Printed or projected 'Don't Miss Out' sidebar text on Xuanzang
periods.visual_aids: Simple sketch-map on the board showing a travel route from China to India and back, with 7th century CE marked

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the Xuanzang sidebar: a Chinese pilgrim who travelled to India in the 7th century CE, spent 17 years visiting scholars and collecting Buddhist texts, and returned to China to translate Sanskrit manuscripts into Chinese. Students then answer: 'What was Xuanzang's purpose in coming to India?' and 'What does a pilgrim-scholar's account offer as historical evidence that an inscription or official record does not?'

The teacher poses two analytical questions for small-group discussion: (a) 'Xuanzang travelled specifically to collect Buddhist texts — what does his journey tell us about India's place in the ancient world as a centre of knowledge?' and (b) 'What kinds of things would Xuanzang notice and record that a Persian military inscription would not?' Groups report back; the teacher records distinctive answers on the board.

Students complete a written source-comparison task: in two columns (Xuanzang's account / Persian inscription), they list two types of information each source would contain and two things each source would NOT tell us. They then write a conclusion sentence: 'For understanding India's cultural influence on China, Xuanzang's account is a better source than a Persian inscription because...'

The teacher draws the connection to the previous unit's Tianzhu insight: the name 'heavenly master' and Xuanzang's 17-year pilgrimage are two different types of evidence pointing to the same historical reality — India's profound cultural and religious significance for ancient China. Students record both evidence types in their notebooks and note the source types each represents.

periods.section_context: Xuanzang, 7th century CE, Buddhist texts, Sanskrit manuscripts, pilgrim account, India-China cultural link
periods.teacher_notes: Having identified Tianzhu as a name encoding India's status as the birthplace of Buddhism, this unit uses Xuanzang's documented journey as a corroborating source of a different type — a pilgrim's account rather than a linguistic derivation. A common confusion: students may treat Xuanzang purely as an interesting story rather than as historical evidence; keep the analytical focus on what his account tells us that other source types cannot. The source-comparison task is the unit's defining cognitive move, requiring students to evaluate source types rather than simply retrieve information from them.

competency_edges.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate what a pilgrim's travel account reveals about cultural relationships that an inscription or official record cannot capture.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understanding India's cultural reach and influence on neighbouring civilisations
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can use a pilgrim's documented journey as evidence for India's role as a centre of Buddhist knowledge in the ancient world.

periods.activity_title: Hindustan and the Full Table: Completing the Foreign-Names Record
periods.section_anchor: How Foreigners Named India — 'Hindustan' in Persian inscription, c. 1,800 years ago / How Foreigners Named India — full foreign-names table ('Let's Explore')
materials: Printed or projected 'Let's Explore' table (Persian, Greek, Latin, Chinese, Arabic and Persian, English, French)
Completed or partial etymology chains from student notebooks
periods.visual_aids: Partially completed foreign-names table displayed on the board with some cells left blank for student completion

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces 'Hindustan': it appears in a Persian inscription about 1,800 years ago and subsequently became the term most commonly used by invaders of India. Students decode it: 'Hindu' (from Sindhu) + 'stan' (Persian suffix meaning land or place). They connect it to 'Hind/Hidu/Hindu' from the Persian unit and note that 'stan' appears in many country names they know (Afghanistan, Pakistan, etc.).

The teacher displays the 'Let's Explore' table (rows: Persian, Greek, Latin, Chinese, Arabic and Persian, English, French) with some cells already filled from what the class has studied. Working individually, students use their accumulated framework notes and etymology chains to complete as many cells as they can — filling in names, roots, and source-language derivations. After individual work, pairs compare and fill gaps collaboratively.

The class completes the table together on the board. For each row, the teacher asks: 'Is this name a direct derivation from Sindhu, or does it pass through an intermediary language? What is the chain?' Students evaluate which names in the table share the Sindhu root and which, if any, do not, and discuss what that pattern tells us about how India became known to the world through its northwest waterway.

Students write a closing two-sentence synthesis in their notebooks: 'Most foreign names for India derive from a single root — Sindhu — because...' and 'The name Bharat survived alongside India because...' The teacher invites one or two responses and closes the chapter.

periods.section_context: Hindustan, Persian inscription, 1800 years ago, foreign-names table, Latin, Arabic, French, English
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the Sindhu chain through Persian, Greek, and Chinese, this unit completes the chapter by adding Hindustan and the full table of foreign names — consolidating the entire foreign-naming thread. A common confusion: students may not realise that English 'India' and French 'Inde' both trace back to the same Greek root (Indoi/Indike), which itself traces to Sindhu; make this explicit when completing the table. The two-sentence synthesis at the close asks students to hold both the Indian and foreign naming threads simultaneously — the chapter's final analytical demand.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why the earliest recorded name for the Subcontinent was regional rather than pan-subcontinental.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Indians Named India — Rig Veda and 'Sapta Sindhava'
assessment_items.question_text: The Rig Veda calls the northwest region 'Sapta Sindhava', meaning the land of the seven rivers. What does this tell us about how the authors of the Rig Veda understood the Indian Subcontinent?

options.label: A
options.text: They knew and named the entire Subcontinent as a single unit.

options.label: B
options.text: They named only the region they inhabited near the Sindhu river, not the whole Subcontinent.

options.label: C
options.text: They believed the Subcontinent had no rivers beyond the northwest.

options.label: D
options.text: They borrowed the name from Persian travellers who had mapped the region.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the Rig Veda's regional naming scope with the pan-subcontinental awareness seen only in later texts like the Mahabharata.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads 'seven rivers' as a claim about the absence of other rivers, rather than as a regional identifier for the northwest.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates the direction of borrowing — the chapter establishes that Persians derived their name from the Indian 'Sindhu', not the reverse.

options.text: Greeks heard the name directly from Indian traders at sea ports.

options.label: B
options.text: Greeks dropped the initial 'H' because that sound did not exist in Greek, transforming the Persian 'Hindhu' into 'Indoi'.

options.label: C
options.text: Greeks invented an entirely new name for India based on their own geographical observations.

options.label: D
options.text: Greeks borrowed the name 'Indoi' from the Chinese term 'Yindu'.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Step | Name used | Language | Derived from
1 | Sindhu | Indian (Sanskrit) | —
2 | Hindhu | Persian | Sindhu (S→H sound shift)

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find reading multi-column tables difficult may be allowed to have the chain read aloud; the reasoning question is still accessible.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the route of transmission — the chapter establishes Greeks received the name via Persian records, not through direct Indian sea contact at this stage.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misses the chapter's central etymological argument that all foreign names trace to a single Indian root; suggests Greeks named independently.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the direction of the chain — Chinese Yindu is a later adaptation from the same root, not a source for the Greek name.

competency.competency_text: Tracing changes in names over historical time

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a chronological chain showing how a name travelled from ancient texts to a modern constitutional document.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Indians Named India — 'Bharat' in the Indian Constitution
assessment_items.task: Build a 'Name Journey' cause-and-effect map showing how the name 'Bharata/Bharat' travelled from its earliest appearance to the Indian Constitution. For each step in the journey, show: the name used, the source it appears in, the type of source, and what changed or stayed the same between that step and the one before it. Your map must include at least four steps and end with Article 1 of the Indian Constitution.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Step 1 — Earliest appearance: Name: ___ | Source: ___ | Source type: ___ | What it referred to: ___
Step 2 — Name in epic literature: Name: ___ | Source: ___ | Source type: ___ | Change from Step 1: ___
Step 3 — Name in a Purana verse: Name: ___ | Source: ___ | Source type: ___ | Change from Step 2: ___
Step 4 — Name in the Constitution: Name: ___ | Source: Article 1, Indian Constitution | Source type: Legal document | Change from Step 3: ___
Conclusion sentence: 'The name Bharat persisted across thousands of years because...'
format_of_output: A cause-and-effect map with at least four labelled steps, each containing the name, source, source type, and a change/continuity note.
A concluding sentence explaining the persistence of the name.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the map format may list the four steps as numbered paragraphs; the content requirements remain identical. Pair work is permitted if the teacher judges it beneficial for accessibility.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: This task requires students to synthesise the entire Indian-naming thread of the chapter by constructing a multi-step causal chain — identifying sources, classifying their type, and articulating continuity and change at each transition. It directly demonstrates the ability to trace how a name travelled from ancient oral/literary contexts to a modern legal document.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold breaks the task into four discrete steps, each requiring four pieces of information, to prevent students from producing a list of names without analytical connection. The conclusion sentence requires a causal explanation, not a summary. Teachers should check that students are writing 'change from previous step' rather than simply restating the name.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses correctly place 'Bharata' in the Rig Veda (as a Vedic group name), trace it through Bharatavarsha in the Mahabharata, the Vishnu Purana's geographical definition, and Article 1 of the Constitution; they articulate what changed (from a group name, to a country name, to a legal name) and what stayed the same (the root 'Bharata'). Weak responses list the names without explaining the type of source or the nature of change at each step, or conflate literary and epigraphic sources.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the task's core cognitive demand is showing how one thing led to another across time — not comparison (which a table serves) or spatial reasoning (which an annotated map serves). The teacher may substitute any other format from the menu (comparison table, annotated diagram, source analysis task, structured discussion with written output) if a different format better suits the class.

competency.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify a named ancient text as a historical source and explain what kind of evidence it provides about a region.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Indians Named India — Rig Veda and 'Sapta Sindhava'
assessment_items.question_text: The Rig Veda uses the term 'Sapta Sindhava' for the northwest region. As a historical source, what kind of evidence does the Rig Veda provide about ancient India that a stone inscription cannot?

options.label: A
options.text: It provides official government records of territories controlled by ancient rulers.

options.label: B
options.text: It provides evidence of the names, language, and geographical awareness of the people who composed it, preserved in oral and literary tradition.

options.label: C
options.text: It provides exact dates and measurements of the regions it describes.

options.label: D
options.text: It provides foreign observers' descriptions of the Subcontinent from outside.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses a literary/religious text with an epigraphic or administrative record — a confusion the chapter directly addresses by distinguishing source types.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Attributes the precision of modern cartographic sources to an ancient literary text; conflates the kind of knowledge different source types can produce.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the Rig Veda (an internal Indian source) with foreign travellers' accounts — the chapter's two main categories of evidence.

competency.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate what a pilgrim's travel account reveals about cultural relationships that an inscription or official record cannot capture.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Foreigners Named India — Xuanzang sidebar ('Don't Miss Out')
assessment_items.question_text: Xuanzang, a Chinese pilgrim, travelled to India in the 7th century CE, spent 17 years collecting Buddhist texts, and returned to translate Sanskrit manuscripts into Chinese. Why is Xuanzang's account a useful historical source for understanding ancient India's relationship with China, beyond what a Persian inscription about 'Hindustan' can tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: A pilgrim's account is always more accurate than an inscription because it is based on personal experience.

options.label: B
options.text: Xuanzang's account records India's role as a living centre of Buddhist knowledge — the cultural and intellectual reasons why a Chinese scholar would travel there — which an inscription recording a geographical name cannot convey.

options.label: C
options.text: Xuanzang's account proves that Persian inscriptions are unreliable as historical evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: A pilgrim's account replaces the need for inscriptions when studying ancient India.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Overgeneralises source reliability without considering what each source type is designed to record; misses the chapter's point about different source types offering different kinds of evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Sets up a false hierarchy between source types — the chapter treats different source types as complementary, not competitive in reliability.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misunderstands the chapter's argument: sources are valued for what they distinctively reveal, not for replacing one another.

competency.competency_text: Interpreting named source types to build historical understanding

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare what a literary source and an epigraphic inscription each reveal about the geographical conception of the Subcontinent.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Indians Named India — Bharatavarsha, Jambudvipa, and Ashoka's inscription
assessment_items.question_text: The Mahabharata (a literary text) uses the term 'Jambudvipa', and Emperor Ashoka (c. 250 BCE) used the same term in a stone inscription. Compare what each source type reveals about ancient Indians' geographical conception of the Subcontinent. What can Ashoka's inscription tell us that the Mahabharata cannot, and vice versa?
expected_elements: The Mahabharata, as a literary source, shows that the concept of Jambudvipa existed in the cultural and narrative imagination of ancient Indians — it names the whole Subcontinent in a storytelling tradition.

Ashoka's inscription, as an epigraphic/official source, shows that a ruling emperor used the same term as an administrative designation for his empire — confirming the term had real political currency, not only literary use.
The Mahabharata cannot confirm whether the term was used in governance; Ashoka's inscription cannot tell us the cultural or mythological associations the term carried in popular imagination.
Together, the two source types show the term was both culturally embedded and politically applied.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use a simple two-column format (literary source / inscription) if prose comparison is a barrier.

competency.competency_text: Mapping textual geographical descriptions onto physical geography

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can locate ancient regional names from a historical text onto an outline map and match them to contemporary geographical areas.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Indians Named India — Mahabharata regional names and Fig. 5.4
assessment_items.question_text: The Mahabharata lists 'Pragjyotisha' as one of the regions of the Subcontinent. Based on the chapter, which present-day region does 'Pragjyotisha' roughly correspond to?

options.label: A
options.text: Parts of Bengal

options.label: B
options.text: Today's Kutch

options.label: C
options.text: Roughly today's Assam

options.label: D
options.text: Parts of Haryana

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses Pragjyotisha with Vanga — Bengal's Mahabharata name; a confusion between two eastern regions listed in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses Pragjyotisha with Kaccha — the Mahabharata name for today's Kutch; a confusion between geographically distant regions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses Pragjyotisha with Kurukshetra — the Mahabharata name for parts of Haryana; a confusion between the chapter's most prominent named region and a less familiar one.

competency.competency_text: Mapping textual geographical descriptions onto physical geography

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate whether a textual geographical boundary description matches the physical features of the Indian Subcontinent.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Indians Named India — Vishnu Purana verse and geographical boundaries
assessment_items.question_text: The Vishnu Purana verse says: 'The country that lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is called Bharata.' Which of the following best evaluates whether this description accurately matches the physical geography of the Indian Subcontinent?

options.label: A
options.text: The description is completely accurate because the Himalayas are to the north and the Indian Ocean is to the south of the Subcontinent.

options.label: B
options.text: The description captures the major north-south boundaries correctly — Himalayas in the north, ocean in the south — but does not mention the eastern and western oceans, which an ancient Tamil poem adds.

options.label: C
options.text: The description is inaccurate because the Subcontinent has deserts and plains, not just mountains and oceans.

options.label: D
options.text: The description only applies to north India and ignores the peninsular south entirely.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Accepts the verse as complete without noticing that it omits the eastern and western oceanic boundaries — a failure to evaluate, rather than simply recall.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies an irrelevant criterion (interior landscape features) to a boundary description; misunderstands what geographical boundary descriptions are designed to specify.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misreads 'south of the snowy mountains' as restricting the definition to north India, rather than understanding it as defining the northern limit of a territory that extends to the southern ocean.

competency.competency_text: Understanding India's cultural reach and influence on neighbouring civilisations

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a foreign name for India encodes a cultural relationship, not only a geographical derivation.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Foreigners Named India — Chinese names: Yintu, Yindu, Tianzhu
assessment_items.question_text: The Chinese used two types of names for India: 'Yintu/Yindu' (derived phonologically from Sindhu) and 'Tianzhu' (which could be read as 'heavenly master'). What does the use of 'Tianzhu' tell us about the Chinese relationship with India that 'Yintu/Yindu' alone does not?

options.label: A
options.text: It tells us that China and India shared the same language in ancient times.

options.label: B
options.text: It tells us that the ancient Chinese regarded India with cultural and religious reverence as the birthplace of the Buddha, not merely as a geographical location.

options.label: C
options.text: It tells us that Chinese rulers controlled parts of the Indian Subcontinent.

options.label: D
options.text: It tells us that Chinese scholars disagreed about what India should be called.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses cultural exchange with linguistic identity — a shared name derivation does not imply a shared language.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses cultural reverence (evidenced by the name's meaning) with political control — the chapter describes India as a centre of pilgrimage and learning for China, not a political dependency.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Misreads the coexistence of multiple names as disagreement, rather than as different names serving different purposes (phonological vs. cultural).

competency.competency_text: Understanding India's cultural reach and influence on neighbouring civilisations

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a pilgrim's documented journey as evidence for India's role as a centre of Buddhist knowledge in the ancient world.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Foreigners Named India — Xuanzang sidebar ('Don't Miss Out')
assessment_items.question_text: Xuanzang, a Chinese pilgrim, travelled from China to India in the 7th century CE and spent 17 years visiting scholars and collecting Buddhist texts before returning to translate Sanskrit manuscripts into Chinese. Which conclusion about India's role in the ancient world is best supported by these facts?

options.label: A
options.text: India and China had no cultural contact before the 7th century CE.

options.label: B
options.text: India was regarded as a significant centre of Buddhist learning, important enough for a Chinese scholar to make a 17-year journey to study there.

options.label: C
options.text: China produced no Buddhist texts of its own and depended entirely on India for all religious knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: Xuanzang's journey proves that Buddhism originated in China rather than India.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Contradicts the evidence directly — the chapter establishes that the name Tianzhu and Xuanzang's journey both attest to long-standing India-China cultural contact.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overstates the conclusion — the chapter supports India's prominence as a centre of Buddhist learning, not China's total dependence on India for all religious knowledge.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the chapter's evidence — Xuanzang travelled to India precisely because Buddhism originated there and Sanskrit Buddhist texts were held there.
